question: What primary structures on the surface of red blood cells determine an individual's blood group?
explanation: Blood groups are classified based on specific inherited antigenic substances located on the red blood cell membrane. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why does the human immune system react against foreign red blood cell antigens during an incompatible transfusion?

options.A: It recognizes the foreign antigens as non-self and attacks them
options.B: It converts the donor red blood cells into white blood cells
options.C: It immediately destroys the recipient's own healthy platelets
options.D: It absorbs the extra volume and triggers fluid overload

explanation: The immune system uses self-recognition mechanisms to identify foreign markers and mounts a defensive antibody response against them. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which antibodies are naturally present in the plasma of a person with Type A blood?
explanation: According to ABO principles, individuals have antibodies in their plasma against the antigens they lack on their red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: A patient with Type AB blood has which specific characteristics regarding antigens and antibodies?

options.A: Only B antigens on cells with anti-B antibodies in the plasma
options.B: No antigens on cells with both anti-A and anti-B plasma antibodies
options.C: Both A and B antigens on cells with no plasma ABO antibodies
options.D: Only A antigens on cells with anti-A antibodies in the plasma

explanation: Type AB blood expresses both major antigens on the erythrocyte membrane and contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies in the serum. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h2)

question: When do individuals with Rh-negative blood typically develop anti-Rh antibodies?

options.A: After exposure to Rh-positive red blood cells
options.B: Whenever they are exposed to Type O blood products
options.C: During early embryonic development in the womb
options.D: Naturally within the first six months of life

explanation: Anti-Rh antibodies are not naturally occurring; they form only after immune system exposure to the foreign D antigen. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: What makes the Rhesus blood group system distinct from the ABO system regarding plasma antibodies?

options.A: Rh-negative individuals lack natural circulating anti-Rh antibodies until sensitized
options.B: Rh antibodies are only found in the platelets rather than the blood plasma
options.C: Rh blood types rely entirely on cellular immunity instead of immunoglobulins
options.D: Rh-positive individuals carry both anti-A and anti-Rh antibodies simultaneously

explanation: Unlike ABO antibodies which develop spontaneously in early life without prior exposure, Rh antibodies require sensitization to manifest. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of reverse blood grouping in a laboratory setting?

options.A: To detect the exact volume of hemoglobin present in the donor sample
options.B: To confirm plasma antibodies by mixing serum with known red blood cells
options.C: To separate white blood cells from platelets prior to crossmatching
options.D: To sterilize the blood collection bag using chemical reagents

explanation: Reverse grouping uses known red blood cells to verify that the antibodies found in the patient's serum match their forward group. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: During a major crossmatch procedure, what exact components are combined together in the test tube?

options.A: Donor plasma and recipient white blood cells
options.B: Recipient platelets and donor whole blood
options.C: Donor serum and patient saline solution
options.D: Recipient serum and donor red blood cells

explanation: A major crossmatch specifically tests the recipient's serum against donor red blood cells to catch any pre-formed antibodies that could destroy the donor cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which blood type is considered the universal red cell donor in emergency clinical scenarios?
explanation: Type O negative red blood cells lack A, B, and RhD antigens, minimizing the risk of a severe acute hemolytic reaction in un-typed recipients. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why can an individual with Type AB positive blood safely receive red blood cells from almost any ABO/Rh donor group?

options.A: Their red blood cells contain antibodies that neutralize donor plasma
options.B: Their immune system is temporarily suppressed during transfusions
options.C: Their bone marrow instantly adopts the donor's genetic blood type
options.D: Their plasma lacks antibodies against A, B, and Rh antigens

explanation: Because Type AB positive plasma contains no anti-A, anti-B, or anti-Rh antibodies, it will not attack incoming donor red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h5)

question: What pathological process characterizes an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Destruction of donor red blood cells by recipient antibodies
options.B: Massive depletion of circulating platelets causing petechiae
options.C: Severe allergic bronchospasm triggered by plasma proteins
options.D: Sudden bacterial proliferation inside the stored blood bag

explanation: Mismatched transfusion leads to immediate immune-mediated lysis of the infused red blood cells by the recipient's circulating antibodies. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary mechanism behind hemolytic disease of the newborn in Rh-incompatible pregnancies?

options.A: Maternal platelets migrate into the fetal circulation and cause clotting
options.B: The infant's liver fails to conjugate bilirubin due to premature birth
options.C: Maternal IgG anti-D antibodies cross the placenta and lyse fetal red blood cells
options.D: Fetal white blood cells attack the mother's bone marrow stem cells

explanation: Sensitized Rh-negative mothers produce small, placental-crossing IgG antibodies that target the D antigens on fetal red blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h6)
